_README: This is the only file you edit to update your publications.
1. Add an entry to the 'papers' list below. Copy an existing one and change it.
'id' must be unique - use lastname+year, e.g. 'abeykoon2027'.
2. Put the DOI in 'doi' - just the bare DOI, e.g. 10.1029/2023JB026710
The site turns it into a working link automatically. 'url' is only for
papers with no DOI; leave it empty otherwise.
3. Add the same id to the 'papers' list of whichever theme it belongs to.
Your own name is highlighted automatically wherever it appears.
Themes show in the order listed here; the archive is sorted newest first.

themes.label: Theme one
themes.title: Deep inside: metal, sulphur and the fluids that move things
themes.summary:
Sulphur is a quiet, ordinary element that turns out to control a great deal. Down where the Earth's mantle meets its core, it decides which metals stay behind and which sink with it, and it leaves traces inside diamonds as trapped inclusions that we can read as a thermometer. Much shallower, in the upper mantle and the crust, water and other fluids move upward through rock in ways that are very hard to observe directly.

This was the work of my doctorate and the years around it. Much of it meant recreating the conditions rather than finding them: a new way to trap and read a fluid, using a trap made from a pair of single-crystal diamonds; a new geothermometer from the oxygen inside sulphide inclusions; and a neutron beam in Japan aimed at iron sulphide to find out where hydrogen actually sits inside it at high pressure and temperature.

themes.label: Theme two
themes.title: How magma flows, and why that decides everything
themes.summary:
Whether a volcano flows or explodes comes down, to a surprising degree, to how sticky its magma is. Viscosity governs how fast melt rises, whether gas can escape gently or builds until the rock shatters, and therefore what an eruption does to the people living near it.

Measuring it is harder than it sounds, because the thing you want to measure changes while you measure it. A lot of this work has been about the method itself — calibrating a calorimetric approach so that different laboratories get the same answer, and tying viscosity to the actual atomic structure of the melt. The volcanoes involved are ones with history: Campi Flegrei, Colli Albani, Etna.

themes.label: Theme three
themes.title: Crystals, textures and the moment an eruption turns
themes.summary:
Magma is rarely a simple liquid. It carries crystals, and those crystals grow, dissolve and rearrange as it rises - changing how the whole mixture behaves on timescales short enough to matter during an eruption.

This work looks at how quickly crystals appear, what delays them, and what the resulting textures can tell us afterwards. Some of it is done in real time at a synchrotron, watching a sample as it changes rather than examining it after the fact.

themes.label: Theme four
themes.title: Seeing small
themes.summary: A recurring thread through all of it: finding ways to look at things that are too small, too fast, or too deep to observe by ordinary means. Sometimes that means adapting an electron microscope to reveal individual defects in a crystal; sometimes it means building a new sample assembly so an experiment survives the pressure at all.

themes.label: Earlier work
themes.title: Water, land and the people who depend on them
themes.summary:
Before the deep Earth, there was water. My earliest research was environmental geochemistry in Sri Lanka and South India - tracing how seawater intrudes into a coastal aquifer, following trace elements through suburban waterways, and contributing to the long, difficult question of the kidney disease of uncertain origin affecting farming communities in Sri Lanka's dry zone.

It is a different field from the one I work in now, but not a different instinct. It was the same question asked at the surface: what is moving through this rock, and what does it mean for what lives on top of it?
